The museum includes important exhibits such as antiquities from Harappan times, gold coins of Chandragupta, and various copper and bronze implements.

(August 2023) (Learn how and when to remove this message) Shillong was the capital of composite Assam during the British regime and for a quarter century in independent India until a separate State of Meghalaya was formed 1972. David Scott, the British civil servant of the East India Company, was the Agent of the Governor-General North East Frontier. During the First Anglo-Burmese War the British authorities felt the need for a road to connect Sylhet and Assam. The route was to traverse across the Khasi and Jaintia Hills. David Scott overcame the difficulties his administration faced from the opposition of the Khasi Syiems – their chiefs and people. Impressed by the favourable cool climate of Khasi Hills, they negotiated with the Syiem of Sohra in 1829 for a sanatorium for the British. Thus began the consolidation of British interests in the Khasi-Jaintia Hills. In early 1829, a Khasis confederation mounted a serious uprising against British occupation. But by January 1833, their leader Tirot Sing surrendered to David Scott and was detained to Dacca (present-day Dhaka). A political agent was posted in Sohra, also known as Cherrapunjee. But the British did not like the climate and facilities of Sohra and they moved to Shillong. "Ïewduh" is the biggest market in Shillong. The name "Shillong" was later adopted, as the location of the new town was below the Shillong Peak. In 1874, a separate Chief Commissionership was formed with Shillong as the seat of administration. The new administration included Sylhet, now a part of Bangladesh. Also included in the Chief Commissionership were the Naga Hills (present-day Nagaland), Lushai Hills (present-day Mizoram) as well as Khasi, Jaintia and Garo Hills. Shillong was the capital of composite Assam till 1969 when the autonomous state of Meghalaya was formed. In January 1972, Meghalaya was made a full-fledged state.[1] The Shillong Municipal Board dates back to 1878, when a proclamation was issued constituting Shillong and its suburbs, including the villages of Mawkhar and Laban, into a station under the Bengal Municipal Act of 1876. Inclusion of the villages of Mawkhar (S.E. Mawkhar, Jaiaw and part of Jhalupara and Mawprem) and Laban (Lumparing, Madan laban, Kench's Trace and Rilbong) within the Municipality of Shillong was agreed to by Haiñ Manik Syiem of Mylliem under the agreement of 15 November 1878.[2] But, there is no trace of Shillong in the British era maps dating back to 1878, up to 1900. - **History**: Built in 1442 during the Ming dynasty, the observatory underwent significant reorganization in the 17th century by Jesuit astronomers, who introduced new and more accurate instruments. It played a crucial role in the observation of celestial bodies for the emperors of the Ming and Qing dynasties.

- **Significance**: The observatory was essential for astronomical observations and assisted in navigation, with contributions from Muslim scholars. It is recognized as a significant cultural and historical site.

- **Access**: The observatory is located just south of Jianguomen in Dongcheng District and can be accessed via the Beijing Subway (Lines 1 and 2) and various bus routes.

- **Additional Information**: For more details, you can visit the [Wikipedia page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing_Ancient_Observatory).

sections.title: History
sections.content: History[edit] An image of the observatory after reorganization by the Jesuits The layout of the observatory It was said that in 1227, the Jin dynasty transferred the ancient astronomical instruments from Kaifeng to the first observatory in Beijing. In 1279, the succeeding Mongols under Kublai Khan built a new observatory just north of the current observatory. Kublai Khan made his chief adviser of hydraulics, mathematics and astronomy, Guo Shoujing, director of the observatory in 1283 after the death of Guo's friend and predecessor Zhang Wenqian.[1] After the Mongols, Zhu Yuanzhang, the founding Ming Emperor, transferred the instruments from Beijing to Nanjing. When the Yongle Emperor came to power, he had craftsmen make copies of the instruments in Nanjing and sent them to the Beijing observatory. The current observatory was completed in 1442. It assisted the Ming and Qing astronomers in their observation reports for the Emperor. As he was considered the "Son of Heaven", the movements of the heavenly bodies were an important affair. Another function was to assist sea navigation, with Muslim scholars recruited for their expertise in the area.[citation needed] In the mid-17th century, after winning an astronomy contest, the Jesuit Ferdinand Verbiest was awarded complete charge of the astronomy observatory by the emperor. In 1673, he supervised the rebuilding of some of the instruments. He and other Jesuits helped to further develop the observations of the stars and the planets. During the later stages of the Qing dynasty, members of the Eight-Nation Alliance looted some of the instruments. However, as World War I drew to a close, the instruments were returned to China by the French and German governments. An early seismograph of Zhang Heng's design used to be housed at the observatory. sections.title: History
sections.content: History[edit] An image of the observatory after reorganization by the Jesuits The layout of the observatory It was said that in 1227, the Jin dynasty transferred the ancient astronomical instruments from Kaifeng to the first observatory in Beijing. In 1279, the succeeding Mongols under Kublai Khan built a new observatory just north of the current observatory. Kublai Khan made his chief adviser of hydraulics, mathematics and astronomy, Guo Shoujing, director of the observatory in 1283 after the death of Guo's friend and predecessor Zhang Wenqian.[1] After the Mongols, Zhu Yuanzhang, the founding Ming Emperor, transferred the instruments from Beijing to Nanjing. When the Yongle Emperor came to power, he had craftsmen make copies of the instruments in Nanjing and sent them to the Beijing observatory. The current observatory was completed in 1442. It assisted the Ming and Qing astronomers in their observation reports for the Emperor. As he was considered the "Son of Heaven", the movements of the heavenly bodies were an important affair. Another function was to assist sea navigation, with Muslim scholars recruited for their expertise in the area.[citation needed] In the mid-17th century, after winning an astronomy contest, the Jesuit Ferdinand Verbiest was awarded complete charge of the astronomy observatory by the emperor. In 1673, he supervised the rebuilding of some of the instruments. He and other Jesuits helped to further develop the observations of the stars and the planets. During the later stages of the Qing dynasty, members of the Eight-Nation Alliance looted some of the instruments. However, as World War I drew to a close, the instruments were returned to China by the French and German governments. An early seismograph of Zhang Heng's design used to be housed at the observatory. Deekshabhoomi is a sacred monument of Navayana Buddhism located in Nagpur, Maharashtra, India. It is historically significant as the site where B. R. Ambedkar, along with approximately 400,000 followers, embraced Buddhism on 14 October 1956, a day celebrated as Ashoka Vijaya Dashami. This event marked a pivotal moment in the revival of Buddhism in India and is particularly important for the Dalit Buddhist movement.

- The site symbolizes the mass conversion of Dalits to Buddhism, led by Ambedkar, who sought to escape the caste system.
- Ambedkar's choice of Nagpur was intentional, as it was historically significant for the propagation of Buddhism in India.
- Following the conversion ceremony, Ambedkar's movement continued to inspire millions, leading to further conversions even after his death in December 1956.

**Further Information:**  
For more details, you can visit the [Wikipedia page on Deekshabhoomi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deekshabhoomi).

Dr. Ambedkar had declared in 1935 that although he was born as a Hindu, he would not die as one,[1] as conversion was the solution to abandon the caste system.[2] After this declaration and having extensively and exhaustively studied the doctrines of all the major world religions, Dr. Ambedkar would choose Buddhism for himself and his followers.[2] Buddhism was 2,550 years old in 1956, so it was a notable year of celebration for the Buddhist religious world globally and 14 October was the traditional date of conversion of Emperor Ashoka, the great Indian Buddhist Monarch and the day is celebrated as Ashok Vijaya Dashmi.[3] He selected Nagpur for his conversion ceremony, as he explained in his speech at that occasion, because Nagpur was the homeland of 'Nag' people who embraced Buddhism, supported it with great efforts in its early period, and propagated it throughout India.[4][5] Ground near the Ramdaspeth area in Nagpur was selected for the ceremony. On 14 October 1956, Dr. Ambedkar and his wife took the oath of Three Jewels and Five Precepts from the Burmese monk Mahasthavir Chandramani from Kushinagar.[6][7] Dr. Ambedkar then gave the oath of Three Jewels, Five Precepts, and 22 Vows to thousands of his followers.[6] In this way, Nagpur became the birthplace of Neo Buddhist movement.[8] Dr. Ambedkar died on 6 December 1956, one and a half months after the Deeksha ceremony. However, this ceremonial conversion continued after his death, converting 15-20 million by March 1959.[9] After his death the 'Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar Deekshabhoomi Smarak Samiti' (Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar Deekshabhoomi Memorial committee) was organized for the management of Deekshabhoomi. The committee decided to build a stupa at the place as a monument of that ceremony and a mass conversion of people to Buddhism. Dr. Ambedkar had declared in 1935 that although he was born as a Hindu, he would not die as one,[1] as conversion was the solution to abandon the caste system.[2] After this declaration and having extensively and exhaustively studied the doctrines of all the major world religions, Dr. Ambedkar would choose Buddhism for himself and his followers.[2] Buddhism was 2,550 years old in 1956, so it was a notable year of celebration for the Buddhist religious world globally and 14 October was the traditional date of conversion of Emperor Ashoka, the great Indian Buddhist Monarch and the day is celebrated as Ashok Vijaya Dashmi.[3] He selected Nagpur for his conversion ceremony, as he explained in his speech at that occasion, because Nagpur was the homeland of 'Nag' people who embraced Buddhism, supported it with great efforts in its early period, and propagated it throughout India.[4][5] Ground near the Ramdaspeth area in Nagpur was selected for the ceremony. On 14 October 1956, Dr. Ambedkar and his wife took the oath of Three Jewels and Five Precepts from the Burmese monk Mahasthavir Chandramani from Kushinagar.[6][7] Dr. Ambedkar then gave the oath of Three Jewels, Five Precepts, and 22 Vows to thousands of his followers.[6] In this way, Nagpur became the birthplace of Neo Buddhist movement.[8] Dr. Ambedkar died on 6 December 1956, one and a half months after the Deeksha ceremony. However, this ceremonial conversion continued after his death, converting 15-20 million by March 1959.[9] After his death the 'Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar Deekshabhoomi Smarak Samiti' (Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar Deekshabhoomi Memorial committee) was organized for the management of Deekshabhoomi. The committee decided to build a stupa at the place as a monument of that ceremony and a mass conversion of people to Buddhism. ### Shorsky National Park

**Overview:**
Shorsky National Park is a protected area located in southwestern Siberia, where the West Siberian Plain meets the South Siberian Mountains. It is characterized by its forested, mountainous terrain and dark taiga tree cover. Established in 1999, the park spans an area of approximately 1,614 square miles (4,180 km²), covering over a third of the Tashtagolsky District in Kemerovo Oblast, about 300 kilometers south of the city of Kemerovo. The park is home to the indigenous Shors people and has a history linked to mining and logging industries before its designation as a protected area.

**Key Features:**
- **Location:** Tashtagolsky District, Kemerovo Oblast, Russia
- **Established:** 1999
- **Area:** 1,614 square miles (4,180 km²)
- **Flora and Fauna:** The park features diverse ecosystems, including dark taiga forests, which are home to various wildlife species.

**Historical Significance:**
The Shors people have traditionally inhabited this region, known for their iron-smelting skills and practices of Shamanism. The area has transitioned from active logging to conservation, allowing the mature forests to thrive.

**Best Season to Visit:** Summer

**Further Information:**
- [Wikipedia - Shorsky National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shorsky_National_Park)

This park offers a unique opportunity to experience the natural beauty and cultural heritage of Siberia, making it a worthwhile destination for nature enthusiasts and those interested in indigenous cultures.

query: Hukou Waterfall is the largest waterfall on the Yellow River and the world's largest yellow waterfall. It is located at the intersection of Shanxi and Shaanxi provinces in China.
answer:
I have confirmed that Hukou Waterfall is indeed a significant attraction, and I found additional waterfalls in China, but they don't seem to be as relevant as the Hukou Waterfall itself.

### Final Information on Hukou Waterfall (壶口瀑布)

- **Location**: Intersection of Shanxi and Shaanxi provinces, China.
- **Significance**: It is the largest waterfall on the Yellow River, the second largest waterfall in China, and the world's largest yellow waterfall.
- **Dimensions**: 
  - Width: Typically 30 meters (98 ft), increasing to 50 meters (164 ft) during flood season.
  - Height: Over 20 meters (66 ft).
- **Description**: The waterfall forms as the Yellow River approaches the Hukou Mountain, where the river is narrowed by mountains on both sides. The water's velocity increases and plunges over a narrow opening on a cliff, creating a dramatic waterfall effect, likened to water pouring from a huge teapot.

### Additional Information
- **Wikipedia**: [Hukou Waterfalls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hukou_Waterfalls)
- **Visual Tags**: Waterfall, valley, mountain, China, panoramic views.

result.historical_summary: The Hukou Waterfalls is the largest waterfall on the Yellow River, the second largest waterfall in China, and the world's largest yellow waterfall. It is located at the intersection of the provinces of Shanxi and Shaanxi, 165 km (103 mi) to the west of Fenxi County, and 50 km (31 mi) to the east of Yichuan County where the middle reaches of the Yellow River flow through Jinxia Grand Canyon. The width of the waterfall changes with the season, usually 30 metres (98 ft) wide but increasing to 50 m (164 ft) during flood season. It has a height of over 20 m (66 ft). When the Yellow River approaches the Hukou Mountain, blocked by mountains on both sides, its width is abruptly narrowed down to 20–30 m (66–98 ft). The water's velocity increases, and then plunges over a narrow opening on a cliff, forming a waterfall 15 m (49 ft) high and 20 m (66 ft) wide, as if water were pouring down from a huge teapot. Hence it gets the name Hukou Waterfall.

SELECT DISTINCT
            e.viewpoint_id,
            e.name_primary,
            e.name_variants,
            e.category_norm,
            e.popularity,
            0.0 as name_score,
            1.0 as geo_score,
            CASE WHEN e.category_norm IN (%s,%s) THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END as category_score
        FROM viewpoint_entity e
        WHERE viewpoint_id IN (
                    SELECT DISTINCT viewpoint_id 
                    FROM viewpoint_visual_tags 
                    WHERE tags @> %s::jsonb
                    
                    
                )
        ORDER BY e.popularity DESC NULLS LAST
        LIMIT %s
